***Prince of Persia*** is a [video game franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_franchise "Video game franchise") created by [Jordan Mechner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Mechner "Jordan Mechner"). It is centered around a series of [action-adventure games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action-adventure_games "Action-adventure games") focused on various incarnations of the eponymous [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_(Prince_of_Persia) "Prince (Prince of Persia)"), set in ancient and medieval [Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persia "Persia").

The first two games in the series, *[Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_(1989_video_game) "Prince of Persia (1989 video game)")* (1989) and *[Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_2:_The_Shadow_and_the_Flame "Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame")* (1993), were published by [Broderbund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broderbund "Broderbund"). *[Prince of Persia 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_3D "Prince of Persia 3D")* (1999), named for being the first installment to use [3D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"), was developed by [Red Orb Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Orb_Entertainment "Red Orb Entertainment") and published by The Learning Company on [PC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer"); the [Dreamcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") version was developed by [Avalanche Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche_Software "Avalanche Software") and published by [Mattel Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel_Interactive "Mattel Interactive"). [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft") bought the rights to the franchise in 2001 and [rebooted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reboot_(fiction) "Reboot (fiction)") it with *[Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time")* (2003). Ubisoft has since developed and published five additional entries in the series: *[Prince of Persia: Warrior Within](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_Warrior_Within "Prince of Persia: Warrior Within")* (2004), *[Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Two_Thrones "Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones")* (2005), *[Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_(2008_video_game) "Prince of Persia (2008 video game)")* (2008), *[Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Forgotten_Sands "Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands")* (2010), and *[Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Lost_Crown "Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown")* (2024), as well as a number of spin-offs and games for mobile devices (by [Gameloft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft "Gameloft")). A remake of *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* was announced in 2020, but it was cancelled at the beginning of 2026.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Outside of the games, the franchise includes a [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time_(film) "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time (film)"), a graphic novel and the *[Lego Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Prince_of_Persia "Lego Prince of Persia")* toyline. Ubisoft's *[Assassin's Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's_Creed "Assassin's Creed")* franchise is considered to be the [spiritual successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_successor "Spiritual successor") to the series.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Original trilogy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Original trilogy")]

The first game in the series was created by [Jordan Mechner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Mechner "Jordan Mechner") after the success of *[Karateka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karateka_(video_game) "Karateka (video game)")*. Drawing from multiple general sources of inspiration, including the *[One Thousand and One Nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Thousand_and_One_Nights "One Thousand and One Nights")* stories,[[5]](#cite_note-PoPhistory1-5) and films like *[Raiders of the Lost Ark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raiders_of_the_Lost_Ark "Raiders of the Lost Ark")*[[6]](#cite_note-6) and *[The Adventures of Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Robin_Hood_(film) "The Adventures of Robin Hood (film)")*,[[7]](#cite_note-GDC2011-7) the protagonist's character animation was created using a technique called [rotoscoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotoscoping "Rotoscoping"), with Mechner using his brother as the model for the titular prince.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The original *Prince of Persia*, with its more than 20 platform [ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porting#Porting_of_video_games "Porting"), is one of the most ported games in video game history.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Mechner enrolled in [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University")'s film department, producing an award-winning short film during his time there, before returning to design and direct a sequel to the original game.[[11]](#cite_note-PoPhistory2-11) The sequel, *Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame*, was developed internally at Broderbund with Mechner's supervision. The game, like its predecessor, received critical acclaim and high sales. Broderbund was subsequently purchased by [The Learning Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Learning_Company "The Learning Company"),[[12]](#cite_note-CNET-12) which was later acquired by US game company [Mattel Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel_Interactive "Mattel Interactive").[[13]](#cite_note-LC_Mattalmerger-13) In 1999, *[Prince of Persia 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_3D "Prince of Persia 3D")* was developed and released under Broderbund's Red Orb label.[[11]](#cite_note-PoPhistory2-11) Released for PC and the Dreamcast only,[[14]](#cite_note-14) it was criticized by many users as being buggy, and was a commercial disappointment.[[11]](#cite_note-PoPhistory2-11) The Broderbund/Learning Company's games division, the assets of which included the *Prince of Persia* franchise, was subsequently sold to [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft").[[15]](#cite_note-LCpurchase-15)

### *The Sands of Time* series

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Sands of Time series")]

Mechner, who owned the *Prince of Persia* [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property"), was brought in to work with Ubisoft on a reboot of the franchise, titled *[The Sands of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time")*, although he was originally wary after the failure of *Prince of Persia 3D*.[[16]](#cite_note-PoPhistory3-16) The team they worked with was also working on *[Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Clancy's_Splinter_Cell_(video_game) "Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell (video game)")*: their aim with the game was to "breathe new life into the action-adventure genre".[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Mechner did not take part in the production of the next game, *[Prince of Persia: Warrior Within](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_Warrior_Within "Prince of Persia: Warrior Within")*, and he commented on finding the dark atmosphere and heightened level of violence unappealing.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The changes also provoked mixed reactions from critics, but sales were strong and a third game, eventually titled *[Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Two_Thrones "Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones")*, went into production.[[20]](#cite_note-PoPhistory4-20) For *The Two Thrones*, the developers and artists tried to strike a balance between the light, cartoon-like tones of *The Sands of Time*, and the grittier mediums of *Warrior Within*.[[21]](#cite_note-TTbalance-21)

A fourth installment in *The Sands of Time* series, *[Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Forgotten_Sands "Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands")*, was released in May 2010.[[22]](#cite_note-PoP_FS-22) The Windows, [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") and [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") versions of the game filled in some of the narrative gap between *The Sands of Time* and *Warrior Within*, whereas the PSP, Wii, and the DS versions each feature their own alternative storylines. The game was released as a tie in to [*The Sands of Time*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time_(film) "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time (film)") film adaptation.[[23]](#cite_note-GameTiming-23)

#### Trilogy collection

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Trilogy collection")]

The *Prince of Persia Trilogy* (known as *Prince of Persia Trilogy 3D* on the remastered collection's title screen) is a collection of *The Sands of Time* trilogy released on the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") and subsequently on the [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") as part of the [Classics HD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classics_HD "Classics HD") range.[[24]](#cite_note-24) The collection includes *The Sands of Time*, *Warrior Within* and *The Two Thrones*, all previously released on the PlayStation 2, [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_(console) "Xbox (console)") and [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"). The games were remastered in high-definition for the PlayStation 3 with [3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopy "Stereoscopy") and [PlayStation Network Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Network_Trophies "PlayStation Network Trophies") support on one [Blu-ray Disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc "Blu-ray Disc"). The PlayStation 2 collection was released on October 27, 2006, in Europe,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] while the remastered collection was released on November 19, 2010, on Blu-ray in [PAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PAL "PAL") regions. The release marks the first Classics HD title to not be published by [Sony Computer Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Computer_Entertainment "Sony Computer Entertainment").

In North America, the three games were originally released separately as downloadable-only titles on the [PlayStation Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Store "PlayStation Store"). The first, *The Sands of Time*, was released on November 16, 2010, while the other two games followed in December.[[25]](#cite_note-25) The Blu-ray version was to be released in North America on March 22, 2011[[26]](#cite_note-26) but the collection ended up being delayed until April 19.

### *Prince of Persia* 2008 reboot series

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Prince of Persia 2008 reboot series")]

In 2006, concept designs surfaced hinting at another entry in the franchise.[[27]](#cite_note-27) The game, titled simply *[Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_(2008_video_game) "Prince of Persia (2008 video game)")*, is a second reboot of the franchise, with its level and combat design harking back to the original 1989 game.[[28]](#cite_note-ubidaysinterview-28) The game was released in December 2008, receiving positive reviews from most video game outlets and decent sales.[[29]](#cite_note-29) Alongside the main game, Ubisoft's Casablanca branch developed a direct sequel and spin-off for the Nintendo DS, titled *[Prince of Persia: The Fallen King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Fallen_King "Prince of Persia: The Fallen King")*,[[30]](#cite_note-FallenKingAnnounced-30) which received fair reviews.[[31]](#cite_note-IGNreview-31)[[32]](#cite_note-gamespotreview-32)[[33]](#cite_note-1UP_Review-33)[[20]](#cite_note-PoPhistory4-20)

### Spin-offs and remakes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Spin-offs and remakes")]

The first spin-off of the series was developed alongside and released in the same year as *The Two Thrones* for the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS"). *Battles of Prince of Persia* is a turn-based strategy game set between *The Sands of Time* and *Warrior Within*.[[34]](#cite_note-BoPoP-34) It received mediocre reviews from critics.[[35]](#cite_note-BPoPmeta-35)[[36]](#cite_note-BPoPGamerank-36)

In 2007, [Gameloft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft "Gameloft") and [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft") released *[Prince of Persia Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_Classic "Prince of Persia Classic")*, an enhanced remake of the original [*Prince of Persia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia_(1989_video_game) "Prince of Persia (1989 video game)") for [Java ME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_ME "Java ME"), [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)"), [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS"), [Xbox 360 (XBLA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Live_Arcade "Xbox Live Arcade"), and [PlayStation 3 (PSN)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Network "PlayStation Network").[[37]](#cite_note-37) It is developed by Gameloft's internal studio [Gameloft Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft_Montreal "Gameloft Montreal").[[38]](#cite_note-38) The visual style was upgraded to resemble *[Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time")*, and the Prince himself was given some additional moves, such as the ability to roll, backflip, wall jump and stop time briefly during combat. However, the core gameplay remains the same as the original – the player must defeat Jaffar within one hour while watching out for the many traps and defeating the guards they encounter.

There have been a number of [mobile games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_games "Mobile games") for Java ME-based phones developed by [Gameloft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft "Gameloft"), some based on older PC or console titles with 2D graphics and others loosely based on contemporary games but with 2D graphics and different gameplay due to technology constraints. Gameloft has also developed some ports for both the [iPhone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone "IPhone") and the [iPad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPad "IPad").[[39]](#cite_note-PoP_retro-39) The first spin-off by Gameloft was titled *Prince of Persia: Harem Adventures*, released for Java phones in 2003.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Specifically, the company has developed (via its [Gameloft Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft_Montreal "Gameloft Montreal") studio) HD remakes of the original *Prince of Persia* in 2007,[[41]](#cite_note-41) and its sequel (via [Gameloft Pune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameloft_Pune "Gameloft Pune"), a studio which now belongs to Ubisoft) *The Shadow and the Flame* in July 2013.[[42]](#cite_note-PoP2remake-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44)

In 2018, [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft") under the banner of its entity [Ketchapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketchapp "Ketchapp") released *Prince of Persia: Escape*,[[45]](#cite_note-45) a mobile game for Android and iOS. It is a [runner game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runner_game "Runner game") made up of different levels,[[46]](#cite_note-46) and the player can customize the protagonist with outfits from past games. Reviewing for *[Pocket Gamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_Gamer "Pocket Gamer")*, Cameron Bald called *Prince of Persia: Escape* a "mundane game crushed under the weight of excessive greed".[[47]](#cite_note-47) In August 2022, a follow-up, *Prince of Persia: Escape 2*, was released.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

In January 2024, Ubisoft released the first major installment in the series since *The Forgotten Sands*, *[Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Lost_Crown "Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown")*. It is a [2.5D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2.5D "2.5D") [side-scrolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side-scrolling "Side-scrolling") [platformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platformer "Platformer") and introduces a new storyline and protagonist, Sargon, a member of the [Immortals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immortals_(Achaemenid_Empire) "Immortals (Achaemenid Empire)").[[49]](#cite_note-49)

*The Rogue Prince of Persia* is a 2.5D [roguelike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roguelike "Roguelike") title developed by Evil Empire and released on August 20, 2025 on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox Cloud, and PC – through Ubisoft Connect, Steam, and the Epic Games Store – and will be coming to Switch 2 and Switch later in 2025. The game entered development around 2019, after a discussion between Evil Empire and Ubisoft at [GDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Developers_Conference "Game Developers Conference"), and its art direction is heavily inspired by Franco-Belgian comics. The game was Ubisoft's first day-one [Steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_(service) "Steam (service)") release in five years, as well as their first title to be released in Early Access before a full release.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

## Canceled and unreleased games

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Canceled and unreleased games")]

### *Prince of Persia Redemption*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Prince of Persia Redemption")]

In 2012, leaked images from a project entitled *Osiris* were assumed to be the next *Prince of Persia* title.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Jordan Mechner even commented on his Twitter account that the images were not from a *Prince of Persia* game.[[52]](#cite_note-52) A year later, Yannis Mallat, CEO of [Ubisoft Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft_Montreal "Ubisoft Montreal"), said that the franchise was being "paused", saying that "as soon as we have something to show, we will".[[53]](#cite_note-53) In the following months, Ubisoft confirmed that it was either planning or considering next-generation entries in multiple franchises, including *Prince of Persia*.[[54]](#cite_note-POPconsidered-54) A video uploaded by a Ubisoft Montreal artist in 2012 but only discovered in 2020 showed a gameplay trailer for *Prince of Persia Redemption* which would have been released for Windows, Xbox 360, and PlayStation 3.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)[[57]](#cite_note-57) According to Jonathan Cooper, a former Ubisoft animator at the time, the trailer was a mockup of the planned gameplay for the title created by Khai Nguyen, used to pitch the game concept. The game never developed beyond that point, though the work on the pitch trailer was used to prepare a similar trailer for *[Assassin's Creed III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's_Creed_III "Assassin's Creed III")*.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

### *The Sands of Time* remake

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: The Sands of Time remake")]

A remake of the *Sands of Time*, formally announced at Ubisoft Forward 2020, was originally scheduled for release on January 21, 2021, for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One, but Ubisoft delayed the remake indefinitely.[[59]](#cite_note-59) In its quarterly financial report, Ubisoft stated that the remake was expected to be out sometime during its 2022–23 fiscal year.[[60]](#cite_note-60) The remake's development was moved to Ubisoft Montréal, a change from [Ubisoft Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft_Mumbai "Ubisoft Mumbai") and Ubisoft Pune. The company said the 2023 fiscal year release target was no longer being targeted.[[61]](#cite_note-61) A new release window of 2026 was announced at Ubisoft Forward 2024.[[62]](#cite_note-62) Ubisoft officially canceled the remake on January 21, 2026 with the announcement of a major restructuring of the company.[[63]](#cite_note-63)

## Adaptations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Adaptations")]

### Graphic novel

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Graphic novel")]

Jordan Mechner finished writing the story for a graphic novel in 2007. The novel was written by A.B. Sina, and illustrated by Alex Puvilland and [LeUyen Pham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeUyen_Pham "LeUyen Pham"). It was released by [First Second Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Second_Books "First Second Books") in autumn 2008.[[64]](#cite_note-64)[[65]](#cite_note-65) The story follows two Princes, jumping between the 9th and 13th centuries. Although it belongs to the franchise the plot is not related to any of the game continuities or that of the 2010 film.[[66]](#cite_note-66)

### Film adaptation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Film adaptation")]

Main article: [*Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time_(film) "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time (film)")

In 2010, a film adaptation of *[The Sands of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Sands_of_Time "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time")* was released by [Walt Disney Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Pictures "Walt Disney Pictures"). Starring [Jake Gyllenhaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Gyllenhaal "Jake Gyllenhaal") as Prince Dastan, it would go on to receive mixed reception, but still gross $336 million in theaters.[[67]](#cite_note-mojo-67) Besides *The Sands of Time*, the film also incorporated elements from *[Warrior Within](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_Warrior_Within "Prince of Persia: Warrior Within")* and *[The Two Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Persia:_The_Two_Thrones "Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones")*, the two other titles from the *Sands of Time* trilogy of the *Prince of Persia* video game franchise.

Upon the film's release, it was accompanied by *Before the Sandstorm*, a 2010 one-shot comic book published by [Disney Publishing Worldwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_Publishing_Worldwide "Disney Publishing Worldwide"). This comic serves as both a direct prequel and sequel to the feature film, and explains the motives and backgrounds of some characters. It was written by Jordan Mechner and featured illustrations by [Todd McFarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_McFarlane "Todd McFarlane"), [Niko Henrichon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niko_Henrichon "Niko Henrichon"), [David Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lopez_(artist) "David Lopez (artist)") and [Bernard Chang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Chang "Bernard Chang").

### Lego

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Lego")]

[Lego Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Prince_of_Persia "Lego Prince of Persia") was released by [The Lego Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lego_Group "The Lego Group") in 2010, as part of the company's strategy to produce sets based on Disney properties.[[68]](#cite_note-LADIDFTSCPOPK-68) Based on the feature film, Lego released six sets within the theme, as well as a short animated film, before discontinuing it.[[69]](#cite_note-BrickLink-69)[[70]](#cite_note-harvest_moon_snes-70)

## Reception

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Awards

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Awards")]

The success of the *Prince of Persia* series resulted in [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") awarding the series six world records in the *Guinness World Records: Gamer's Edition 2008*. These records include First Motion-Capture Animation in a Video Game and Highest Rated Platformer on PS2 and Xbox.

### Impact and legacy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prince_of_Persia&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Impact and legacy")]

South Korean singer-songwriter Kim Kwang-Jin released the song 'Magic Castle', with lyrics inspired from the storyline of the original *Prince of Persia*.[[71]](#cite_note-71)

In 1992, Russian author [Victor Pelevin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Pelevin "Victor Pelevin") wrote a book called *A Werewolf Problem in Central Russia and Other Stories*, in which there is a short story called "Prince of Gosplan". The story is greatly influenced by the game; the main hero of the story lives in a mixed reality of the real world and video games and identifies himself as Prince of Persia. He tries to understand if his life is real or if he is just seeing it on a computer display.[[72]](#cite_note-PrincePelevin-72)

The feel of the gameplay in *[Tomb Raider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_Raider "Tomb Raider")* was intended to evoke that of the original *Prince of Persia*.[[73]](#cite_note-TRsecrets-73)

The *[Assassin's Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's_Creed "Assassin's Creed")* series originated out of ideas for a sequel for *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time*. Its critical and financial success led Ubisoft to request [Ubisoft Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft_Montreal "Ubisoft Montreal") to develop a sequel, aiming for the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") and [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3"). The Ubisoft Montreal team decided on taking the gameplay from *The Sands of Time* into an [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") approach, taking advantage of the improved processing power to render larger spaces and crowds. Narratively, the team wanted to move away from the Prince being someone next in line for the throne but to have to work for it; combined with research into secret societies led them to focus on the [Assassins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Assassins "Order of Assassins"), heavily borrowing from the novel *[Alamut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamut_(Bartol_novel) "Alamut (Bartol novel)")*.[[74]](#cite_note-polygon_oral-74) They developed a narrative where the player would control an Assassin that served as a bodyguard for a non-playable Prince, leading them to call this game *Prince of Persia: Assassin*. The "Animus" device allowed them to explain certain facets of gameplay, such as accounting when the player fails a mission, in the same way they had done in *The Sands of Time*.[[74]](#cite_note-polygon_oral-74)
